name: Dayanidheeswarar Temple, Tiruvadakurangaduthurai
deity: Shiva as Dayanidheeswarar (also Valeeswarar), with the goddess Jata Makuta Nayaki
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine on the northern bank of the Kaveri, sung in the Tevaram (7th century); first structure traditionally traced to the Pallava age, rebuilt by Pandya and Chola patrons
dynasty: Pallava origins; rebuilt by Pandya and Chola patrons
summary: Dayanidheeswarar, the Lord who is a treasure of compassion, is worshipped at the Tiruvadakurangaduthurai of the Tevaram on the Kaveri's northern bank, where tradition says the monkey heroes of the Ramayana, Vali and Hanuman, came to pray.

sections.history: On the northern bank of the Kaveri, in the delta country near Thiruvaiyaru, stands Tiruvadakurangaduthurai, praised by the child-saint Sambandar in the Tevaram and so counted a Paadal Petra Sthalam. The name can be read as the northern riverside of the monkeys, and it sets this shrine apart from Thenkurangaduthurai, its namesake on the southern bank, whose monkey tradition is a different story. Local tradition traces a first structure to the Pallava age, later rebuilt by Pandya and Chola patrons, and inscriptions of the Chola period are found within the temple. The village is today often called Aduthurai Perumal Koil, a name that helps travellers tell it from the other Aduthurai near Kumbakonam.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east beneath a five-tiered gateway tower. The main shrine is laid out in three parts: the sanctum, an ardha mandapa before it, and a long maha mandapa that receives the devotee. Above the sanctum rises a three-tiered vimana, described in local accounts as nagara in its form and crowned by a vesara-style crown. The goddess Jata Makuta Nayaki, whose name speaks of the crowned and matted locks, is honoured in a separate sanctum of her own. Among the carvings is a bas-relief of Vali worshipping Shiva, which gives the temple its second name, Valeeswarar.
sections.legends: The temple keeps two Ramayana memories. In one, Rama, Hanuman and their companions were journeying south when they came to this bank of the Kaveri, which served as a crossing. To make the river passage safe, Hanuman prayed to Shiva here and set up the lingam known as Dayanidhi, the Lord of compassion. A second telling says Hanuman came to atone for having harmed the lingam of sand that Sita had made at Rameswaram. The other legend is Vali's. All his might was said to lie in his tail, and when it was wounded as he struck at Ravana, the strength left it. Vali came here and worshipped Shiva until his power was restored, and so the Lord is also remembered as Valinathar.
sections.festivals: The goddess Jata Makuta Nayaki receives special adornment and worship on every full-moon day, when devotees gather in good numbers. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed as at every Shiva temple, and the Tamil-month festivals are kept in the manner of the Kaveri delta. Dates follow the Tamil calendar, so confirm them locally before travelling.
sections.experience: Tiruvadakurangaduthurai is a quiet, unhurried temple set among the green fields of the Kaveri delta. Enter beneath the five-tiered gateway, walk the long mandapa to the sanctum of Dayanidheeswarar, and look for the small relief of Vali at prayer before going on to the goddess in her own shrine. Devotees come in particular to ask for strength restored after illness or setback, in the spirit of the Vali story, and many time their visit for a full-moon evening. The temple is best combined with the other Tevaram shrines around Thiruvaiyaru.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: The temple lies in the Kaveri delta of Thanjavur district, on the northern bank of the river near Thiruvaiyaru. Thanjavur and Kumbakonam are the nearest large towns with railway stations, and Tiruchirappalli has the nearest airport. Local buses and autorickshaws reach the village from Thiruvaiyaru; ask for Aduthurai Perumal Koil to avoid confusion with the other Aduthurai near Kumbakonam.
